strengths: Novel theoretical framework using real-analyticity to prove almost-sure injectivity of transformer language models with rigorous measure-theoretic arguments
Exceptionally thorough empirical validation: 5 billion+ pairwise comparisons across six SOTA models with zero observed collisions, plus exhaustive stress tests on 343+ billion similar prompt pairs
Provably correct algorithm (SIPIT) with linear-time guarantees achieving 100% exact recovery empirically, significantly outperforming baselines in efficiency (28s vs 3889s)
Finite-horizon guarantee that injectivity persists through gradient descent training, not just at initialization—technically non-trivial result using absolute continuity preservation
Clear presentation with elegant mathematical framework, complete proofs in appendix, and thorough reproducibility details
Significant implications for interpretability (validates information encoding in last-token states), privacy/compliance (embeddings retain full text content), and mechanistic interpretation research
Clever witness construction in proofs that explicitly demonstrates parameter configurations preventing collisions
weaknesses: Gap between theory and practice: real-analyticity assumptions may not hold for quantized models, finite-precision arithmetic, non-smooth activations, or non-standard training procedures (Adam, momentum, learning rate schedules)

Collision threshold (10^-6) appears arbitrary without sensitivity analysis; unclear how floating-point precision (10^-7 to 10^-16) relates to threshold; no robustness studies on numerical precision effects

SIPIT has practical limitations: requires access to hidden layer activations (not exposed in deployed APIs), needs gradients for efficient gradient-guided policy (incompatible with black-box access), requires causal attention throughout architecture

Limited scope: analysis restricted to decoder-only models; last-token injectivity only (not full sequence or earlier positions); finite context assumption; no coverage of encoder-decoder or vision-language variants

Incomplete treatment of failure modes: brief mention of tied embeddings and equal positional encodings, but inadequate discussion of how common these violations are in modern models or other subtle architectural variants
Theoretical step size constraint η ∈ (0,1) for gradient descent stated without justification or tightness analysis; unclear how this relates to practical learning rate schedules
Limited experimental ablations: no robustness testing to noise in hidden states, no quantized model analysis, limited exploration of very long sequences, no study of different initialization schemes
HARDPROMPTS comparison may be unfair (designed for vision-language models); insufficient positioning relative to recent LLM interpretability and input-recovery attack literature
